standard.title: Locating and Organising Information
standard.description: locate, select and organise information, data and ideas from different sources
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can locate, collect and organise information and data from primary and secondary sources in a range of formats (AC9HS6S02). The Y7 shift is to civics-specific source types (government websites, specialist reports, legislation) and a more deliberate approach to source selection and organisation.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students locate, select and organise information, data and ideas from different sources relevant to political, legal and civic investigations.

nodes.label: Identifying and using civics-relevant sources
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the types of sources relevant to civic investigations (government websites, media, specialist reports, statistics) and explain why different source types are appropriate for different purposes.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least three types of sources useful for civic investigations (e.g. government websites, news articles, specialist reports) and explain what kind of information each provides.
nodes.typical_width: Identify the range of source types relevant to civics — government websites, media reports, articles, graphs, charts, statistics, specialist reports from bodies like the Australian Law Reform Commission — and explain which source types are most appropriate for finding information about government systems, legal principles, cultural diversity, and civic issues.
wider: Evaluate the relative authority of different source types for civic claims — comparing a government website, a newspaper editorial, and a specialist report on the same issue
Investigate how to access official sources such as the Australian Law Reform Commission reports, parliamentary Hansard, and ABS data for civics research
Explore the difference between primary sources (legislation, Hansard, court decisions) and secondary sources (media, commentaries) in a civic research context
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot distinguish between appropriate and inappropriate source types for civic claims, their research (S02) and analysis (S03) will be built on poorly selected evidence. This is the source literacy gate for civic inquiry.

response_modes.reason: Students need a working repertoire of civics-specific source types — not just 'Google it', but knowing when to look at Hansard, ABS, specialist commission reports, or government websites. Practise finding the right type for different question types.

success_criteria: Identify at least three source types relevant to civic investigations and explain what each provides
Match a given inquiry question to the most appropriate source type and explain the choice

nodes.label: Locating information using search strategies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use targeted search strategies including advanced search functions to locate relevant information for civic investigations.
nodes.minimum_width: Use a focused search query (including at least one search strategy beyond a basic keyword search) to locate information relevant to a civic question.
nodes.typical_width: Locate information using advanced search strategies including targeted criteria (e.g. allintext: searches, site: searches, date filters); use online sources effectively to find government websites, reports, statistics and media coverage relevant to civic investigations.
wider: Use multiple search strategies on the same question and compare the results to evaluate which strategy was most effective for finding relevant civic information
Practice locating primary sources directly (e.g. finding legislation on legislation.gov.au, Hansard on aph.gov.au) rather than relying on secondary reporting
Investigate how to evaluate the currency and authority of online sources — practising source evaluation alongside source location

response_modes.reason: Advanced search skills require practice — basic keyword searching is the default and students need repeated opportunities to use more targeted strategies before they become habitual.

success_criteria: Use at least one targeted search strategy beyond basic keywords to locate relevant civic information
Identify an appropriate online source for a given civic research question

nodes.label: Selecting and organising information
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can select information from multiple sources on the basis of similarity and relevance to the investigation topic, and organise it coherently for analysis.
nodes.minimum_width: Select information from at least two different sources that is relevant to a civic inquiry question, and organise it so that similar ideas from different sources are grouped together.
nodes.typical_width: Select and organise information from different sources (media reports, online publications, government websites) on the basis of similarity and relevance; identify key findings from specialist sources such as Law Reform Commission reports; organise information in a format that supports analysis (e.g. comparison table, annotated notes, concept map).
wider: Develop a structured note-taking system that tracks which source each piece of information came from, supporting later citation and attribution
Practice organising conflicting information from different sources — identifying where sources agree and disagree rather than only looking for supporting evidence
Organise information from a civic investigation into a structure that anticipates an argument or explanation, moving from collection to analytical organisation

response_modes.reason: Organising information by similarity and relevance (rather than by source) is a cognitive step that many students skip — practise is needed to build the habit of synthesising rather than summarising.

success_criteria: Select information from at least two sources that is relevant to a civic inquiry question
Organise selected information so that similar ideas from different sources are grouped, not just listed by source
